content: A body bag is a non-porous bag specifically designed to hold a human body. It is primarily used for the storage and transportation of corpses. These bags are also commonly utilized for storing bodies in morgues. Before the advent of purpose-made body bags, cotton mattress covers were sometimes used, particularly in combat zones during the Second World War. However, modern body bags made of rubber or plastic are far superior, as they effectively prevent the leakage of bodily fluids, which often occurs post-mortem. The standard dimensions of a body bag are approximately 36 inches by 90 inches. In contemporary warfare, body bags are frequently employed to contain the remains of deceased soldiers. Governments typically maintain reserves of body bags in preparation for anticipated wars or natural disasters. During the Cold War, large stockpiles of body bags were accumulated in anticipation of mass casualties resulting from potential nuclear warfare. This grim reality was poignantly captured in Adrian Mitchell's protest poem, Fifteen Million Plastic Bags. In films and television, body bags are often depicted as being made of heavy black plastic. However, lightweight white body bags have gained popularity because they make it easier to spot evidence that may have been dislodged from the body during transport. Despite this, black body bags remain widely used, as evidenced by a photograph taken in 2008. Other common colors include orange, blue, and gray. Regardless of their color, body bags are constructed from thick plastic and feature a full-length zipper, which may run straight down the middle or follow a J-shaped or D-shaped path. Some designs include handles (typically two on each side) to facilitate lifting. Information can be written directly onto the plastic surface of a body bag using a marker pen, a practice often employed either at the scene of death or in the mortuary before the body is stored in refrigerated cabinets. Alternatively, some body bags are equipped with transparent label pockets for inserting name cards. In any case, a conventional toe tag can be attached to one of the lifting handles if necessary. Body bags are not designed to be washed or reused, primarily due to hygiene concerns and the risk of contaminating evidence in cases of suspicious deaths. Consequently, body bags are typically discarded and incinerated after a single use. While body bags are most commonly used to transport human remains from the place of discovery to a funeral home or mortuary, they can also serve for temporary burials, such as in combat zones where proper funerals are not feasible due to imminent enemy attacks. For example, during the Falklands War in 1982, British casualties were placed in gray plastic body bags and buried in mass graves. Months after the conflict ended, all remains were exhumed from their temporary graves to receive conventional funeral services with full military honors. The term body bag is sometimes used in a completely unrelated context to describe fashion or utility bags worn on the body, such as sling body bags or cross-body bags. This usage has no connection to the original or medical sense of the term.
